explanations.explanation: Justice is the word, baker. Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says he will ascribe justice to his Maker (Job 36:3). I think he's setting the table before he serves the meal. Everything he says next leans on God being just.

Mystery is a fair guess, because Elihu does say later that God is great, beyond our knowledge (Job 36:26). But here Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says he will ascribe justice to his Maker (Job 36:3). He's backing God up as fair and right. Mystery looks pretty, like a fancy sprinkle that never landed on this cookie.

Anger is a heavy word to hand God, friend, and Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, doesn't do it here. He says he will ascribe justice to his Maker (Job 36:3). He said he's speaking on God's behalf, and what he gives God is justice. Later he even says God does His work in His loving devotion (Job 37:13).

Nope, Elihu says the opposite. He says, “Indeed, God is mighty, but He despises no one…” (Job 36:5). Power and looking down on people are two separate things in his mouth. I've got a big mustache that can lift a whole cookie box, and I still use it to set things down gently.
False is right, baker. Elihu says, “Indeed, God is mighty, but He despises no one…” (Job 36:5). Might and kindness sit in the same sentence. He doesn't let strong turn into stuck-up.

That's it, friend. Elihu says, “…but He enthrones them with kings and exalts them forever.” (Job 36:7). Not just a seat in the room, but a throne next to kings. That beats my old seat in a junk drawer next to the dead batteries.

A city gate is a real place in the Bible, but Elihu doesn't use it here. He says God enthrones the righteous with kings and exalts them forever (Job 36:7). So the seat is beside kings. The gate would have been a much smaller promise.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That one sounds holy, baker, and it would be a fine place to be. But it isn't what Elihu says. He says, “…but He enthrones them with kings and exalts them forever.” (Job 36:7). The picture here is thrones, right alongside kings.

Right on the money, baker. Elihu says, “He opens their ears to correction and commands that they turn from iniquity.” (Job 36:10). So God doesn't just point at the problem. He opens the ears so they can hear it. I could use that when I tell somebody the oven is still hot and they reach in anyway.

Elihu does talk a lot about God's strength, and he calls Him mighty in verse 5. But for people caught in cords of affliction, he says something else. He says God opens their ears to correction and commands that they turn from iniquity (Job 36:10). So it's about listening and turning.

explanations.answer: Leaves them to work it out
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Elihu says, friend. Nobody gets left alone in the dough here. He says God tells them their deeds, opens their ears to correction and commands that they turn from iniquity (Job 36:9-10). God is active the whole way.

Elihu splits this into two roads, baker. If they obey and serve Him, they end their days in prosperity. But if they do not obey, he says they perish by the sword and die without knowledge (Job 36:11-12). So prosperity isn't for both roads. It all hangs on the obeying.

False is right, friend. Elihu says, “If they obey and serve Him, then they end their days in prosperity and their years in happiness.” Then he says, “But if they do not obey, then they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.” (Job 36:11-12). Two roads, two endings, and he doesn't blur them together.

Yes, and it's a twist, baker. Elihu says, “God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression.” (Job 36:15). The hard place itself becomes the way the ears open. I'd have guessed the rescue skips the hard part, so Elihu has me checking my notes.

That would be a nice rescue, friend, the kind where the cookies never even burn. But Elihu is talking about the afflicted, people already in trouble. He says God rescues them by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression (Job 36:15). So the rescue happens in the middle of it.

A messenger is a fine idea, and Minty the dove, one of my cookie cutter kids, would volunteer in a heartbeat. But Elihu doesn't mention one here. He says God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression (Job 36:15).

True, baker. Elihu says, “Be careful that no one lures you with riches; do not let a large bribe lead you astray.” (Job 36:18). Two warnings travel together: the lure of riches and the large bribe. It's like a bill that comes with a second bill stapled to it.

Both warnings are there, friend. Elihu says, “Be careful that no one lures you with riches; do not let a large bribe lead you astray.” (Job 36:18). He gives the riches warning and then adds the bribe. So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: They can't keep Job from distress
explanations.explanation: That's the point, baker. Elihu asks, “Can your wealth or all your mighty effort keep you from distress?” (Job 36:19). It's a question, and the way he puts it, the answer is no. Money and hustle can't hold trouble back, and I've watched a whole payday vanish into one car repair.

explanations.answer: They prove God is still with Job
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, friend, but Elihu doesn't say it. He asks whether Job's wealth or all his mighty effort can keep him from distress (Job 36:19). He's talking about what riches and effort can't do. He isn't using them as proof of anything.

explanations.answer: They should all go to the poor
explanations.explanation: Giving is a good thing in the Bible, but Elihu doesn't tell Job to do it here. He just asks, “Can your wealth or all your mighty effort keep you from distress?” (Job 36:19). The point is that wealth and effort can't hold distress back.

Iniquity is the word, baker. Elihu says, “Be careful not to turn to iniquity, for this you have preferred to affliction.” (Job 36:21). That's his warning to Job. I'd like to hear that one gently, like a friend tapping my shoulder before I touch the hot pan.

Silence is a sneaky guess, friend, but that's not the word Elihu uses. He says, “Be careful not to turn to iniquity, for this you have preferred to affliction.” (Job 36:21). Iniquity is what he warns Job about.

Grief makes sense in a hard story like this, baker. But Elihu doesn't warn Job away from it in this verse. He says, “Be careful not to turn to iniquity, for this you have preferred to affliction.” (Job 36:21). The warning is about iniquity.

Magnify it is. Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says, “Remember to magnify His work, which men have praised in song.” (Job 36:24). Make it bigger in your eyes, that's his idea. Like me staring through a magnifying glass at one perfect chocolate chip and just whispering, wow.

Questioning has its place, baker, and Job has plenty of questions in this book. But Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says something else here. He says, “Remember to magnify His work, which men have praised in song.” (Job 36:24). He's calling Job to lift God's work up.

Hide is almost the opposite, friend. Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says, “Remember to magnify His work, which men have praised in song.” (Job 36:24). Men have praised it in song, so it's meant to be out in the open. I've hidden a burnt cookie behind the oven before, but never God's work.

Rain it is, baker. Elihu says God draws up drops of water which distill the rain from the mist, and the clouds pour it out and shower abundantly on mankind (Job 36:27-28). So he starts with something people see all the time. It's an everyday thing, and he says we can't fully understand it.

I love the stars, friend, because every finished cookie box lights up my sky with one. But Elihu doesn't start there. He starts with God drawing up drops of water and showering the rain on mankind (Job 36:27-28). So his first example is rain from the clouds.

Hail comes with storms, but Elihu doesn't mention it in this stretch. He says God draws up drops of water which distill the rain from the mist, and the clouds shower it abundantly on mankind (Job 36:27-28). So he starts with rain.

Food, baker. Elihu says, “For by these He judges the nations and provides food in abundance.” (Job 36:31). The same sky that rumbles and flashes also provides food in abundance. I'd say that's a lot of good coming out of one loud storm.
Gold is shiny, friend, and I'm standing on a gold base, so I get it. But Elihu doesn't say gold here. He says, “For by these He judges the nations and provides food in abundance.” (Job 36:31).
Wisdom is a good word to reach for in this book, baker. But Elihu doesn't use it here. He says, “For by these He judges the nations and provides food in abundance.” (Job 36:31). The word is food.

Elihu says nothing about lightning landing by luck, baker. He says, “He fills His hands with lightning and commands it to strike its mark.” (Job 36:32). God commands it, and it has a mark. That's a lot more aimed than a dropped bag of flour.

False is right, friend. Elihu says, “He fills His hands with lightning and commands it to strike its mark.” (Job 36:32). So the lightning has a mark and God gives the command. It doesn't just land wherever.

God's voice, baker. Elihu says, “Listen closely to the thunder of His voice and the rumbling that comes from His mouth.” (Job 37:2). So the thunder is something to listen closely to. I'd listen even closer than I do when the timer is about to go off.

Footsteps would make a fun picture, friend, but Elihu doesn't use it. He says, “Listen closely to the thunder of His voice and the rumbling that comes from His mouth.” (Job 37:2). The thunder is His voice.

Chariots show up in other places in the Bible, baker, but not in this verse. Elihu says, “Listen closely to the thunder of His voice and the rumbling that comes from His mouth.” (Job 37:2). In this verse, the thunder is His voice.

True, baker. Elihu says, “For He says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and to the gentle rain, ‘Pour out a mighty downpour.’” (Job 37:6). So God speaks, and the gentle rain becomes a mighty downpour. I can't even get dough to rise when I ask nicely.

It's true, friend. Elihu says, “For He says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and to the gentle rain, ‘Pour out a mighty downpour.’” (Job 37:6). The gentle rain gets told to pour out a mighty downpour. Elihu says exactly that.

explanations.answer: So all men may know His work
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Elihu says, “He seals up the hand of every man, so that all men may know His work.” (Job 37:7). He doesn't spell out how, and I won't either. The reason he gives is that all men may know God's work.

explanations.answer: So no one can fight back
explanations.explanation: That one's a guess, friend, and Elihu doesn't say it. He says, “He seals up the hand of every man, so that all men may know His work.” (Job 37:7). The reason he gives is knowing God's work.

Rest for the fields sounds peaceful, baker, but that's not Elihu's reason. He says, “He seals up the hand of every man, so that all men may know His work.” (Job 37:7). The reason is that all men may know God's work.

God, baker. Elihu says, “By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen.” (Job 37:10). So the freeze comes from His breath. That's a lot of ice from one breath, and I can't even cool a cookie rack that fast.
Winter is a natural guess, friend, since ice is on the table. But Elihu says, “By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen.” (Job 37:10). The breath belongs to God.
Night does get cold, baker, so I see where you're going. But Elihu says, “By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen.” (Job 37:10). He credits God's breath for the ice.

That's the one, baker. Elihu says, “Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion.” (Job 37:13). Even a storm that comes for punishment is tied to His loving devotion. That's a big thing to say, and Elihu says it plainly.

Storms sound angry, friend, so I get the guess. But Elihu says, “Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion.” (Job 37:13). He puts loving devotion there, even for punishment.

Patience is a lovely word, baker, and God is patient. But Elihu doesn't use it in this verse. He says, “Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion.” (Job 37:13). The words are loving devotion.

That's what Elihu is getting at, baker. He asks Job if he knows how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash, and if he understands how the clouds float (Job 37:15-16). The answer he's pointing to is no. He calls them wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge.

explanations.answer: Job should learn to read the sky
explanations.explanation: Reading the sky could be a handy skill, friend, but Elihu isn't giving Job a lesson. He asks if Job knows how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash (Job 37:15-16). He's calling them wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge.

explanations.answer: Job brought on the storm himself
explanations.explanation: Elihu never says that, baker. He asks Job if he knows how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash, and if he understands how the clouds float (Job 37:15-16). He's pointing to God's wonders, not blaming Job for the weather.

Not quite, friend. Elihu asks, “…can you, like Him, spread out the skies, as strong as a mirror of bronze?” (Job 37:18). He's asking it as a question, and the answer he's pointing to is no. That's about as likely as me stamping the whole sky onto a cookie.
False is right, baker. Elihu asks, “…can you, like Him, spread out the skies, as strong as a mirror of bronze?” (Job 37:18). His point is that Job can't. Only God does that.

Yes, baker. Elihu says, “Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case because of our darkness.” (Job 37:19). He says it's their darkness that gets in the way. He's counting himself in with that word we.

Elihu doesn't say that, friend. He says, “Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case because of our darkness.” (Job 37:19). He gives their darkness as the reason, not God refusing to listen.

A witness would be handy in a court case, baker, but Elihu doesn't bring one up. He says, “Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case because of our darkness.” (Job 37:19). Their darkness is the reason he gives.

True, baker. Elihu says, “Out of the north He comes in golden splendor; awesome majesty surrounds Him.” (Job 37:22). After the sun nobody can stare at, he shows God coming in golden splendor. I'm standing on a gold base, and even I know that's a different level of gold.

It's true, friend. Elihu says, “Out of the north He comes in golden splendor; awesome majesty surrounds Him.” (Job 37:22). It comes right after the picture of the sun nobody can gaze at (Job 37:21). So the statement matches the text.

Oppress, baker. Elihu says, “The Almighty is beyond our reach; He is exalted in power! In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress.” (Job 37:23). So power and fairness go together here. Elihu says the Almighty does not oppress.
Speak is a fair guess, since God's voice is all over this passage as thunder. But Elihu says, “In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress.” (Job 37:23). The word he uses is oppress.
Listen sounds like something Elihu might say, friend, but not in this verse. He says, “In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress.” (Job 37:23). The word he uses is oppress.

explanations.answer: He is not partial to the wise in heart
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Elihu says, “Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart.” (Job 37:24). So being wise in your own heart doesn't earn you special treatment. It's a good thing to remember for a stamper who thinks he knows the recipe.

explanations.answer: He hides His counsel from all men
explanations.explanation: Elihu doesn't say that, friend. He says, “Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart.” (Job 37:24). The reason he gives is that God isn't partial to the wise in heart.

That sounds like it could fit, baker, but Elihu doesn't say it here. He says, “Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart.” (Job 37:24). The reason he gives is that God isn't partial to the wise in heart.
